subtopic: PAROLE BOARD
PAROLE BOARD
speechtext: Is the government considering separating the functions of the chairman of the parole board and director of the parole service so that these two be administered by two separate people rather than one person as is now the case?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PAROLE BOARD
speechtext:
The answer is no, because the functions of the chairman of the parole board and the director of the parole service are administered by two separate people. This is in accordance with the organization proposed by the Fauteux report which quotes as follows:
"The chairman of the board should be the chief administrative officer for the purposes of all the operations of the board. The day to day administration of the parole service should be the responsibility of an executive director who should be responsible to the chairman of the board. It would be the responsibility of the executive director to see to the proper investigation of cases and the preparation of material in relation to them for consideration by the board and also the supervision of parolees."

speechtext: Was an agreement entered into with the province of Saskatchewan for the construction of a veterinary college at Saskatoon and, if so, (a) what is the amount of the federal government's contribution towards the cost of same (b) will the college be constructed in time to accommodate students in the fall of 1964?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: SASKATOON
speechtext:
The government has undertaken to contribute 25 per cent of the capital cost of establishing a veterinary college in western Canada, to a maximum of $625,000, the location of the college to be decided by the western provinces. The decision of the western provinces has been to locate the college in Saskatoon at the University of Saskatchewan. The contribution of the government of Canada will, therefore, be available towards the capital cost of a veterinary college at that location.
It is a condition of the federal assistance that students who have completed their first year of veterinary studies at a pre-veterinary course at other institutions be accepted into the second year of veterinary studies at the new college not later than the fall of 1964.

Order. The Secretary of State has raised a question of privilege which in my opinion is not a question of privilege. In anticipation of some advice from the house I took the trouble to prepare a few notes, and I think it might be useful if I put them on the record, with regard to the production of papers.
The general principle concerning the character of papers which may be asked for is set out in May's sixteenth edition, page 270, where it is stated:
Parliament is invested with the power of ordering all documents to be laid before it, which are necessary for its information.
Bourinot's fourth edition, at page 246, states in part as follows:
On the other hand, it is the constitutional right of either house to ask for such information as it can directly obtain by its own order from any department or officer of the government.
Obviously it is impossible for the Chair to scan every notice of motion for papers in an effort to determine whether or not such papers actually exist or whether the papers are in the nature of confidential documents.
Motions for Papers
Indeed there is no rule which states that confidential documents may not be asked for, and in some instances what are ordinarily considered to be confidential documents are tabled. At page 273 of May's sixteenth edition it is stated:
However ample the power of each house to enforce the production of papers may be a sufficient cause must be shown for the exercise of that power; and if considerations of public policy can be urged against a motion for papers, it is either withdrawn, or otherwise dealt with according to the judgment of the house.
Therefore it seems that the duty of the Chair in regard to motions for papers is to decide whether or not a motion is in order from a procedural point of view, and I am of the opinion that this motion is in order from this point of view. In this regard I would like to quote from a statement by Mr. Speaker Beaudoin which is found at page 3014 of Hansard, April 3, 1957. It reads as follows:
The motion that has been placed on the order paper is in order, and that is why I have put it to the house. It is opposed and when it is opposed, according to standing order 47 it must be transferred for debate if desired. This has not been asked for, but it has been asked that the minister should say briefly why he is opposed to the motion. At this moment, therefore, the only duty I have is to put the question to the house and let the house pass judgment on it.
In the same regard, at page 1036 of Hansard, July 11, 1958, Mr. Speaker Michener is reported as having used the following words:
Order. This motion is not debatable. It Is a motion for an order of the house to issue in respect of certain papers. It is not debatable, and the only course is to accept or reject the motion. I am advised by the Clerk that that is the method of disposing of such a motion as this. I ask, then, whether it is the pleasure of the house to adopt the same motion.
As will be seen in Hansard of February 15, 1960, page 1055, Mr. Speaker Michener held the view that his responsibility was to see that the motion was before the house in the proper form, but that the house had to decide by its vote whether or not the document was to be produced, and that it would be improper for the Speaker to substitute his decision for that of the house.
On February 27, 1961, as will be found at page 2442 of Hansard, Mr. Speaker Michener also stated that it was for the house to determine whether such a motion for the production of papers should be withdrawn or whether it should be passed.
Basing my action on those precedents, and on standing order 47, I propose to put the motion and allow the house to make a decision in regard to the production of the papers unless such a motion is either withdrawn, allowed to stand or transferred for debate.

speakeroldname: Hon. Waller L. Gordon (Minister of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill C-95, to amend the Income Tax Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, like other acts to amend the Income Tax Act, this bill is rather long and complex. It is based upon the very detailed resolution that was approved by the house on July 23.

It does not contain anything new, other than a very few refinements of a technical nature, which I shall point out when we come to the discussion of the bill clause by clause; and it does not include anything of a contentious nature that was not debated fully in July. The proposed amendments follow the order of the original act, but taken as a whole, with one or two exceptions, they fall into three main categories.
First there are amendments to close loopholes in the act. Second, there are amendments to provide incentives to industries which are intended to raise the level of production and employment in certain areas of slower growth. Third, there are changes in non-resident withholding taxes designed to reduce the cost of borrowing abroad, and to provide incentives to the foreign owners of Canadian subsidiaries to take in Canadian partners in the years to come.
The exceptions that do not fall into any of these three categories include a proposal which will require corporations to pay their taxes over a period that is more comparable to the payment time table for individuals than at present, and a clause to deal with taxations of estates in bankruptcy. I shall go into these items fully when we come to the respective clauses in the bill.
First I should like to say something about the proposals contained in the first of the three categories mentioned, that is, those that are designed to close tax loopholes. The public, including the business public, tends to lose respect for any tax administration when advantage can be taken freely of obvious loopholes in the law. When the royal commission on taxation submits its report it may be desirable to make extensive changes in the taxing statutes. In the meantime it seems desirable to stop some clear opportunities for tax avoidance, and I should like to mention four examples of what it is intended to do about them.
First it is proposed to discourage the widespread practice of gaining a tax advantage through the operation of lease-option arrangements. Under the present law, taxpayers who have entered into lease-option agreements are allowed to deduct from their taxable income capital cost allowances which sometimes greatly exceed both the amount of the annual rentals and the actual cost of the properties concerned. The joint tax committee of the Canadian Bar Association and the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants has advocated for some time that action should be taken to prevent this.
The second example that I would like to mention is the one that at present provides an opportunity, under the act, for companies which incur losses in one year to carry them

forward and apply them against profits earned during subsequent years.
As a result of this, a practice has developed of trafficking in the shares of companies whose businesses have been discontinued, but which technically have certain tax loss carry forward entitlements. For example, a man with a profitable business may purchase the shares of one of these companies and transfer his prosperous business to it, and having done so he can apply the losses incurred previously, and often in a quite different class of business, against the taxable income of his own business. I suggest that surely this was never the intention of parliament when the original proposal was incorporated in the act, and that this practice should be stopped.
The third and rather glaring example of a tax loophole-and one that has been much talked about-is known as dividend stripping. In the normal course when a company pays a dividend to its shareholders who are individuals, the dividend is taxable in the hands of the recipients. However, in the case of closely held companies it is possible for the shareholders, through a series of transactions often involving the incorporation of one or more new companies, to withdraw the surplus of the original company without payment of any tax. This also is a widespread practice which should be stopped.
A fourth example of ways in which taxes can be avoided or reduced arises because of the lower rate applicable to the first $35,000 of taxable corporate income. A practice has developed of dividing a business enterprise between a number of associated companies, each one of which individually obtains the benefit of the lower rate of taxation.
Mr. Speaker, I do not criticize those who have taken advantage of these loopholes in the past, nor those officials who are responsible for administering the law in its present form. However, I do suggest that when loopholes of this kind are brought to our attention it is the responsibility of parliament to deal with them, and in doing so I do not suggest that any of the necessary amendments should be made retroactive in their effect.
In two cases, that is, in connection with dividend stripping and with associated companies it is proposed that the minister be given some discretion, subject however to the right of appeal either to the tax appeal board or the Exchequer Court. No one likes giving ministers discretion in these matters, and least of all, if I may say so, the minister who is responsible for administering the act; but we have not been able to find any alternative solution pending completion of the
Income Tax Act
studies being undertaken by the royal commission on taxation.
Following receipt of the report of that commission I would hope that the limited ministerial discretion now recommended could be dispensed with, and I may say that in conversation with the chairman of the royal commission I have said that, if it is possible for him to let us have a report on this particular subject, ahead of his main report, it would be very useful to the administration.
The second category of amendments to which I referred earlier provides incentives for increased production and increased employment in certain designated areas which, for one reason or another, have not enjoyed as rapid a rate of growth as others. It is proposed that new manufacturing or processing enterprises located in designated areas of slower growth be exempted from income tax for three years, if any such new enterprise begins commercial operations within 24 months of the date of enactment of this bill.
Such enterprises will be entitled to write off new machinery and equipment in as little as two years, and new buildings over a period of five years; and they may defer this writeoff rental after the expiry of the three year tax exempt period. These are very substantial incentives. It is hoped that they will induce new businesses to locate in areas which for some years have lagged behind the rest of Canada in their development and in employment opportunities. Considerable success has been achieved in other countries by offering inducements to companies to locate in areas of slow growth. I could mention quite a number of them, but I am hoping that the hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett), who has made a study of the subject, will have something to say about it in the course of the debate. I am sure she will be able to do so much more ably than I could.
The third category of amendments to which I referred earlier has to do with the proposed changes in the rates of withholding taxes. There seems to be general agreement on this. We must give priority in all our economic policies to measures that will bring our international transactions on current account into better balance; and, as has been stated on other occasions, the government is determined to do just that. As I say, I think most people in this house and the public generally will agree with this objective. However some people do not accept, or do not accept fully, some of its implications; they seem to think it is a mistake to make any changes in established ways of doing business. But surely, Mr. Speaker, there is no

Income Tax Act
excuse for Canadians any longer to refuse to face the situation with which we are confronted. We simply must reduce our vulnerability to fluctuations in the international flows of capital. We cannot count on continuing to borrow abroad to pay our bills. We simply must bring our international transactions more nearly into balance. This really means that somehow or other we must secure a larger share of the North American market for our products.
As everybody knows, we have a surplus on current account with the rest of the world, and if we are to bring our international accounts into balance we must look to the North American market as the place for increased exports. If we are to do this, we must strive, among other things, to increase our exports of certain manufactured goods. We all know this is not going to be easy. We know that some 60 per cent of Canadian manufacturing is controlled by people who reside outside our borders, and we know that the corresponding percentages of absentee ownership for mining and refining are higher, and that for the petroleum industry it is higher still. We know also that a much higher proportion of our industry is controlled by non-residents of our country than is the case in any other country in the world.
A number of countries impose restrictions of one kind or another upon foreign participation in resident corporations and upon inflows of foreign capital. These include such countries as Sweden, Japan, India, Mexico, Britain to some extent, Switzerland and France. I think everyone will agree that in Canada we have gained a great deal from the parent-Canadian subsidiary company relationships that are so prevalent. This has meant access to new developments, to management know-how and to research facilities. But these parent-subsidiary relationships are a source of real difficulty when it comes to our objective of increasing exports, or even to reducing imports, especially of manufactured goods. This is particularly true in some cases where the Canadian subsidiary is wholly owned by a single foreign company. Often the managers of such subsidiaries have no real authority. The important decisions are made by the parent company. Understandably, the top officials of the parent company set their sights on increasing the volume of business and the profits of the total enterprise. It would be unreasonable to expect them to give the special requirements of the Canadian economy undue priority. It would be unreasonable to expect officials of a parent company, for example, to encourage their Canadian subsidiary to compete with its parent in the parent company's home markets or in other countries in which the
parent company is interested, unless there were clear price and profit advantages in so doing.
It is significant, I think, that people who are connected with partially owned Canadian subsidiaries generally consider that having minority shareholding interests is a good thing for Canada. The managers of these companies usually have more autonomy, and apart from that they must keep in mind the best interests of all their shareholders and not just the largest one. In such cases the Canadian partially owned subsidiary is more likely to be allowed to do things that are in the best interests of our country. This is not always true, but I think it is a reasonably valid generalization.
In the budget speech I outlined the views of the government on how harmonious relations with foreign investors can best be preserved. Amongst other things, I referred to the desirability of foreign investors selling minority interests in their enterprises to Canadians and electing a number of independent Canadian directors to represent these interests. I pointed out, of course, that not even a 25 per cent interest in most new or existing enterprises is something that could be realized overnight. It is an objective to be worked towards over a period of years; and when I say that, I mean quite a long period of years.
There was nothing very new in the code of desirable behaviour that I suggested. The same sort of thing has been said by successive governments. But the ever increasing upward trend in foreign ownership of Canadian companies continues. I suggest to hon. members in all seriousness that the time has come when something more than words is needed.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
To this end the bill includes some incentives and some gentle pressures to broaden the base of ownership of Canadian companies gradually and moderately over a period of years. I have suggested already that I believe this would be helpful in achieving the objective of increasing exports or to some extent replacing imports through Canadian production, and thus reducing the current account deficit in our international transactions.
It has been rightly stated that Canadians are not in a position to purchase a quarter interest in all the Canadian subsidiary companies of all foreign corporations, even if they wished to do so. The necessary capital is not available, that is true; but no one has suggested that such a move would or should take place overnight or that in practice the owners of all Canadian subsidiaries would be willing to make some of their shares

available. What has been suggested is merely that it would be a good thing if over a period of years there was a greater opportunity for some kind of partnership in the direction of companies that conduct their business in this country, and in this way more autonomy for local management.
There is nothing very harsh or punitive in the measures now suggested. To begin with, it is proposed to exempt certain institutions- pension funds are an example-from the nonresident withholding tax on interest payments in connection with new issues of securities. I should have made it clear that I refer to certain institutions outside Canada. The reason for this, of course, is that if these institutions, such as foreign pension plans, can buy our bonds without paying a tax to the Canadian treasury, they are more likely to do so. This will broaden the market for Canadian bonds, and it will also reduce the cost of borrowing by Canadians, when this becomes possible once again, and help to keep interest rates down.
Will this apply only to bonds or will it also apply to equity securities?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am only talking about bonds. I am talking about broadening the market and reducing the cost of borrowing, when this becomes possible once again, and also borrowing abroad once again. Because as all hon. members know, until the legislation dealing with the U.S. interest equalization tax is passed by both houses in Washington there is a virtual shutoff of all borrowing by Canadians in the New York market.
The non-resident withholding taxes on dividends would be reduced from 15 per cent to 10 per cent where foreign parent companies make it possible for Canadians to acquire a small minority interest. The withholding taxes on dividends payable by companies which, for one reason or another, do not wish to do this will be increased from 15 to 20 per cent, but this increase will not go into effect until 1965. I suggest to hon. members that to do less than this by way of incentive or by way of a mild push would surely mean that we did not take this matter seriously. If we mean business Canada must gradually take whatever steps are necessary, even if such steps are not popular in all circles, to regain a greater measure of control over her own economic affairs, including the policy decisions of Canadian corporations. If we do not do this, Canadians may well wake up some day, and perhaps sooner than they think, and find that they have lost control not only of their economic destiny but of their political destiny as well.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words
Income Tax Act
on this bill before it goes to committee and is discussed clause by clause. I would remind the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) that just about one year ago when he sat on this side of the house, namely on November 15, 1962, he then said, as reported at page 1654 of Hansard:
A complete revision of the Income Tax Act is overdue, and I think most hon. members of this house would agree. I hate to think that it is going to be postponed for several years pending the report of the proposed royal commission on taxation.
Then the minister went on to express his regrets at the illness of Mr. Carter, the chairman of the commission. The minister then continued:
However, if the government knows what its objectives are, may I suggest that it should not be difficult for a small group of lawyers and chartered accountants who are familiar with taxation matters to draft a new act in a relatively short time without waiting for the report of the royal commission.
The minister now sits on the other side of the house. He has had the opportunity now to do just what he suggested, but he has brought forward very little except certain amendments to the Income Tax Act, the same as was done last year. He has also said, as he said then, that the Income Tax Act is too complex, too complicated; that it is difficult to understand and there are too many loopholes in it. I could not agree more with him in this respect. As a layman, as a businessman, I find the Income Tax Act and its amendments passed from year to year becoming more complex and difficult for the layman to understand. And here we are, going along the same way, adding more amendments to the act and making it more complicated as time goes on. However, I compliment the minister on closing up some of the loopholes he mentioned, and I think a government is just as responsible as the person who takes advantage of these loopholes, for not having closed them up before they were taken advantage of.
I should like to address my remarks to one section of the act in particular, namely section 16. This is mentioned in the remarks of the minister in the paragraph headed "incentives to industries". As I understand it, the government proposes to give certain substantial concessions to a company which creates a new industry in a designated area. These concessions are threefold. First, these industries will be given a three-year tax holiday from income tax. Second, they will be given a 50 per cent write-off on new machinery which can be completed over a period of two years. Third, they can have

Income Tax Act
a 20 per cent write-off on new equipment and this can be completed over a five year period. I say that these are very substantial incentives, so much so that they have caused great interest and aroused a great discriminatory feeling in the particular area of the country from which I come, southwestern Ontario.
My criticisms on clause 16 are these, and I will try to bring them to the attention of the house without referring to the specific wording of the bill or the clause concerned. This, no doubt, will be done by other speakers in the committee stage. My first criticism would be that this clause is discriminatory. It is discriminatory in its effect because this government did not give sufficient study or attention to working out this incentive program before it was introduced. They did not realize the consequences and the implications of giving this incentive to one particular area in a heavily industrialized region.
When previously discussing the subject in this chamber, I cited the example of a father who had four of his children in a room and who gave to one of them a ten dollar bill while giving the others nothing. Of course, he would have a family row on his hands. This is exactly what the present government has done with regard to this great industrial community. Out of all the cities in this area, they give to one city, the city of Brantford, this particular concession without making it available to the other cities adjacent to it. We have in that area, as a result, a great family row among cities which were members of a very happy family living and working together. We were competitive. There was keen competition among us to get new industries. Then the government asks this house to pass legislation making it possible to grant a concession of this importance to one city and not to another. I say it is absurd for taxpayers to be asked to provide funds to make possible a concession amounting to more than $400,000 for new industry to establish in Brantford, or any other particular city in that area, rather than in, say, Guelph, or some other community.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? Is it true that while this area, Brantford, was being designated, certain industries in Brantford advertised in other neighbouring communities such as Kitchener for skilled labour?

That is precisely true. I understand that was the case in the city of Kitchener. I know that in Galt, only 15 miles from Brantford, one industrialist has intimated that after applying for help in the Brantford area papers not one person from

that area came to apply for a position in a city only 15 miles away.
If this legislation is not discriminatory, why have so many resolutions on the subject been sent to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) and the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) by organizations in Waterloo, Kitchener, Guelph, Galt and other places in this area? Why did a delegation composed of mayors, reeves and other men elected by the people visit Ottawa recently? Why did they come here to put their case before the Minister of Industry, who, I may say, refused to make any changes or concessions with respect to this legislation?
Let us see what the labour council of the city which I have the honour to represent had to say on the subject, as reported in the Mercury of October 11:
If the federal government's policy Is going to be one of offering large subsidies to industry to locate in adjacent municipalities, we have no alternative but to disband our (industrial) commission and rely on a depressed area status.
So in my opinion this is discriminatory legislation of the worst kind. We are given a definition of what constitutes new industry. What is a new industry, under this definition? Well, if I am a manufacturer making a chair in any one of these cities and I put three rungs in it, instead of two, the chair becomes a new product. I have a new industry. I might be running a concern called the dominion chair company of Guelph. All I need to do is move from Guelph, set up in Brantford and call my business the dominion chair company of Brantford. I put up a new factory there, introduce new machinery and become eligible for concessions which amount to as much as $400,000, the amount received in one particular case by an industry which was established in our community and which moved to Brantford in order to take advantage of these substantial benefits.
I know what is probably being said by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the house. They are saying to themselves: he is talking this way just because the shoe pinches. That is not the case at all. I am objecting because, as I say, this legislation is discriminatory. It might be acceptable if it applied to distant places in remote areas where help was needed. I would go along with that, and I am sure other members of the opposition would go along with it, too.
My second ground for criticizing this measure is based on the method used to select the designated areas. The criteria which are used are not fair because they cover the last eight years. It appears that a national employment service area qualifies as a designated area, provided it has been classified by the Department of Labour as a

labour surplus area for half or more of the summer months, May to October, during the past eight years and has experienced an employment increase of less than half of the national average over the same period. There are certain other alternatives set out in various subparagraphs. Statistics are all very well in some cases, but they must have a direct application to the situation we are facing. With regard to the case I have brought to the attention of the house, the case of the city of Brantford, I draw the attention of hon. members to the following which appeared in the Kitchener-Waterloo Record of October 11. Here it is, a full page, with the heading: " 'Distressed' Brantford Blushing But Grateful". There is a picture of park benches with only two people sitting on them. There is another picture of the employment service office-an office with not a soul in it except the officials. There is a picture of the main street of Brantford crowded with people shopping. It gives anything but the appearance of a distressed area. Then the text goes on to say this-and I cite the following in order to show that one cannot depend upon statistics alone:
The city has long leaned heavily on its main industry-farm machinery. And in the past, the two giants, Massey-Ferguson and Cockshutt, have produced at full speed in fall and winter for the ripe spring market. But in summer, they have laid off hundreds.
This is a specific case. There are also, in that area, workers in the tobacco fields who enter the district to help in the planting and harvesting of the crop. Many of these people are transients, but after the tobacco season is finished they remain in the area over the winter. I bring these examples to the government's attention to show that you must use more than statistics in picking out designated or distressed areas.
My third criticism is that this is a very contradictory piece of legislation. Why? We have the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) sitting across from us, who has just said he is going to bring in amendments to the Income Tax Act so that fewer and fewer United States subsidiaries will locate in Canada. He is going to tax them so they will not come into this country, or something like that. This is what the legislation means in laymen's language. He is not going to encourage them to come in here. Now we have his partner, the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury), to whom he is talking at this minute, saying to this United States firm which had decided to locate in Guelph: You go over to Brantford which is a designated area, and we will give you $400,000 on a silver platter. The ministers' actions are contradictory and they are at cross purposes with one another.
Income Tax Act
This seems to be the type of legislative policies we have had ever since the new government came into office, with one minister working against another. Solidarity of the cabinet means nothing any more. Here is a concrete example that they are working at cross purposes.
My fourth criticism is that this legislation overrides municipal and provincial autonomy. The mayor of the city of Brantford did not even know his city was a designated area until this firm went over there and bought a piece of property on which to locate. That was the first he knew about it. Ottawa says to Brantford: You are a designated area, and they had nothing whatever to say about it. This is Liberal central control policy.
Bureaucracy.

Yes. Bureaucracy is the word. Provincial autonomy has been overridden; the Minister of Industry himself has said so. In speaking to the mayor of the city of Guelph he admitted they were overriding the Ontario law which permits no financial concessions to industry. The business of one city outbidding another city for industries got so bad that the province of Ontario said it had to stop and legislation was passed to that effect. It provided that city A could not offer freedom from land tax for five years, and in competition with city A city B could not offer ten years freedom from land tax. This situation was taken care of by the department of municipal affairs in Ontario. Yet the federal government has overlooked this legislation, overridden provincial autonomy and has gone ahead and named Brantford as a designated area.
The psychological effect is very bad. No community likes to be singled out as a slow growing or depressed area. What community wants to be called a depressed area? What community wants to be called a slow growth area? Most municipalities want to stand on their own feet, go it alone and work to develop industrial areas and attract industries in a good, clearcut way, as has been the case in the past.
My fifth criticism is that industrialists are discontented. They dislike having to compete with a new firm that is given concessions and is enticing staff away from them and undercutting prices. The situation is getting to be very bad in Brantford. The controversy has been propelled into the spotlight and new industries are making their contacts with the city through agents, because they do not want to be caught in the glare of publicity.
I hope the Minister of Finance will reconsider this amendment to the Income Tax Act. I summarize my criticisms. First, it is

Income Tax Act
discriminatory. Second, the method of selecting or designating areas is not a sound one. Third, it is contradictory. Fourth, it overrides municipal and provincial autonomy. Fifth, it is very ill conceived and industrialists are not happy about it.
I present these reasons to the house why the amendment should be withdrawn completely. I know that when the Liberals were in opposition they hounded and urged us to introduce tax incentives to increase production and employment. Our government proceeded to lower the rate of tax on profits resulting from increased sales. This was an incentive, but we left it to industry to do it themselves. We did not interfere with municipal or provincial autonomy.
In the particular case to which I have been referring a wealthy United States firm came into my community. They were a well-to-do firm and did not need concessions. They are not poor by any means. In fact, perhaps the situation might be elaborated on in this way by using a Biblical expression: "To him that hath shall be given and to him that hath not shall be taken away even that which he hath". This is a case in point.
For these reasons, and many others which I am sure will be brought before the house before this amendment is passed, I would urge the minister to withdraw the whole section dealing with the proposed tax bonuses to new manufacturing and processing businesses in designated areas, until the matter has been given more careful study. I would beg the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Industry to do this.
Ask the chamber of commerce of Canada what they think about it. Ask the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. Ask the association of mayors and reeves. Ask the experts in the field what they think about this type of legislation. If the minister will approach the people who are close to the problem and if he wants a concrete example I would extend to him a first hand invitation to come to the community I have the honour to represent and learn what the people there are saying and thinking. Only last week end I was visiting the store of the man who ran against me as the Liberal candidate in the 1958 election. He said to me, "Al'f, keep up the fight; you are on the right track and they are wrong". While visiting the fair the other day many of my good Liberal friends said, "You are on the right track and they are wrong; keep up the fight". So I say to the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Industry: Give this discriminatory piece of legislation further and more careful consideration.

Mr. Speaker, in taking part this afternoon in this debate on proposed amendments to the Income Tax Act, I have in mind certain suggestions which I shall be happy to offer to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon). But, before I do so, I should like to point out how the general public and I myself feel about those proposed amendments.
If I am not mistaken, the main intention of the minister, in proposing the amendments, is to enable us to gradually become masters of our own economy. He said himself that the tax changes would help primarily to improve our unfavourable trade balance.
Obviously, there are many ways of achieving that objective. The one we are discussing now, that is the levying of taxes or simply tax exemptions in other areas, is certainly a method which can be used.
We have been told again and again for a long time that no other country's economy is under stronger foreign domination than that of Canada. Such an honour is not too enviable and we should all strive to correct that situation.
The interest Americans have shown for over a century in the expansion of the Canadian economy was certainly not inspired by any concern over the welfare of the Canadian people. Their concern was first to make profits and second, to take over resources which they could easily control and which could provide them, in the years to come, with the raw materials they need for their vast industries.
The fact that the Canadian economy is largely dominated by American interests exerts a tremendous influence on our country's development. As the minister pointed out, when decisions are taken at the management level of those enterprises, in a country other than our own, it is obvious that the concern is not for the human and economic factors involved and which will be affected by the decisions reached. Those people consider the interests of their country in the first place and consequently, the interests of Canada are relegated to the background.
It is therefore urgent, Mr. Chairman, that we take the necessary steps to regain our economic independence.
I pointed out recently that the economic control, the labour control as well as the military and political control, to which we are now subjected, have created lately many problems which are not yet completely solved.
I think that the present government has shown some indications which may lead us to expect that some action will be taken. Enough idle talk, it is time for action.

Mr. Speaker, the budget which was presented to us by the Minister of Finance on June 13 last, showed that he was ready for action, and we were sorry that, at a certain time, he had to back down and even withdraw one of the measures he had advocated, in other words, that he cancelled the tax he intended to impose on the sale of Canadian shares abroad. In my opinion, it was a commendable move, because just a few days after the withdrawal of that tax, we saw that Americans were taking advantage in a hurry of the opportunity which was given to them.
Mr. Speaker, I think that, in future, we shall have to seek further measures in order to promote the development of our industries by Canadians. It is obvious that the most essential measure will probably be the provision of capital, which is clearly inadequate at this time, so that we may take over in some areas which are not ours at present. It is not a matter of depriving those who have investments in Canada. That would not be fair, but we are entitled to buy back our properties and I think that the government should introduce legislation in order to supply the funds that we now need so urgently.
Let the government take the necessary steps so that we may develop our own industry and resources.
From what he said earlier, it seems that the minister's intentions are good and I hope that he will continue to take steps which will bring results.
Mr. Speaker, I urge the minister to give earnest consideration to some of the suggestions that he seemed interested in but that he dares not accept for fear of being considered a joker. In my opinion, the jokers are actually those who, in the past, as well as now, have let our country be developed by foreigners instead of Canadians, letting them benefit, on our behalf, from the natural resources which are so plentiful in our country.

I know that the minister expects very much from the report that will be submitted to him soon by the royal commission on taxation.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder now which measure we should pass in order to keep the control of our Canadian industries and prevent the heads of American industries from taking over Canadian industries established in our country.

It is unfortunate that we should have to take such action against a friendly country, but if it is really friendly, it should understand that control of our economy must be given back to us, along with our political and military control.
Mr. Speaker, before concluding, I wish to mention a point which I particularly have at heart.

Income Tax Act
The Minister of Finance stated earlier, that he was amending the Income Tax Act, in order to remove the so-called "loopholes".
In this connection, I wish to make a suggestion. I admit that it is a rather delicate question to discuss, especially for me, since I come from the province of Quebec. I am referring to the section of the Income Tax Act which provides for a deduction of up to 10 per cent for charitable donations on presentation of official receipts and appropriate evidence.
Mr. Speaker, that is a touchy subject at present in the province of Quebec and I know that there may have been abuses on that point but I am sure that there have been similar abuses, not only among the French-Canadian population of the province of Quebec but in every part of Canada.
I cannot accept that the whole population of my province should be accused of dishonesty because a few people have been using this provision to get a tax rebate. I deny such an accusation, and so that it may not be made again in the future, I urge the minister to have that provision repealed in order that there may no longer be any tax deduction for charitable donations. Now, here is what I would suggest in return: That the tax rate on the $3,000 of taxable income be lowered from 17 to 12 per cent, so as to eliminate all these shenanigans, all that paper work and all those investigators who go about the country and cost the treasury a lot of money.
I see the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Garland) and I ask him to give all his attention to my proposal. As a matter of fact, I think that he did receive a letter I wrote him to this effect. The act lends itself to abuse and, if you think that this legislation is not all it should be, what are you waiting for to change it? I cannot tolerate those continual insinuations to the effect that the people of Quebec are dishonest.
Mr. Speaker, there are hundreds, if not thousands of individuals in the province of Quebec who have made out their income tax returns for 1962 and who are still waiting for the overpaid tax to be reimbursed.
That legislation authorizes deductions of 10 per cent of the taxable income, with suitable evidence of course. Now, if the given proof justifies a certain deduction, why should there be such a delay?
I wonder if it would not be possible to hire other people to conduct other investigations so as to give satisfaction to our fellow citizens.
We are now at the end of October and you will have to pay interest on those amounts you are withholding. That business should be settled once and for all.

Mr. Speaker, I ask the minister, as well as his colleague, to see to it that this section of the act be withdrawn, since it lends itself to abuse. He should accept my suggestion; it would help to simplify an act which is already so complex and confused.
To finish my remarks, let me, strike another note, Mr. Speaker. Our group advocated certain amendments. We made many suggestions and, personally, I consider that with the present taxation system, it is always the consumer who has to pay. It is no good trying to find out who is finally going to pay the tax collected here and there. In the end, it is always the consumer. Why multiply those taxes endlessly?
I therefore ask that the cost of production of the goods sold in this country and the total of taxes levied be indicated. I also ask that taxes be charged on the finished product rather than on all phases of production. That would enable our producers to face competition on foreign markets without risking to be accused of dumping. That would put the Canadian industry in a better position to face foreign competition.
Finally, I think that we could greatly simplify that Income Tax Act because the consumer is always the one who has to pay the bill. Those taxes are levied precisely in order to provide for the payment of the services for which we cannot pay individually and which we are required of the government.
We accept to do our share so that those services may be provided for the majority. So, it is normal that we should accept to pay that premium, if I may call it that, so that the government can keep on providing those services.
This proposal we just put forward today is certainly not the ideal thing, far from it, but it tends to alleviate the taxpayers' burden. I am not a taxation expert and I suppose that those experts could find other alternatives; but, on the other hand, when we depend only on experts, the result is that we get exceedingly complicated situations. I think that this document prepared by experts could be used as conclusive evidence.

Mr. Speaker, what we are dealing with this afternoon is, I suppose, the somewhat battered remnant of the budget that was presented to us many months ago. I would like for a moment to point out that in the modern world of government administration a budget is something far more than merely the housekeeping accounts of our national government. It is a piece of mechanism by which a government decides,

in the first place, just how the national income is going to be distributed. It is a piece of mechanism by which a government can to a great extent determine just how much its revenues shall increase and how much its expenditures can increase, or vice versa.
I have been rather struck with some of the measures in this bill. I was at the time they were introduced in resolution form by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) and on that occasion I suggested that perhaps the budgetary mechanism was not being used in the best interests of the Canadian people. I think we should remember that this budgetary mechanism is the same wherever it operates; it is the piece of mechanism not only by which the Minister of Finance of Canada protects the interests of a number of quite well padded corporations but it is the same sort of mechanism by which his opposite numbers in different parts of the world achieve different purposes. I suppose you might say it is the piece of mechanism by which Mao Tse-tung rather ruthlessly turns Chinese peasants into industrial workers. In the present instance we have in this bill a number of provisions that are going to increase the holdings of rather privileged sections of our society. I say this having regard to statistics that I am sure the minister has seen, which indicate that those sections of our society are doing very well now.
We have, for instance, the report of the dominion bureau of statistics with regard to gross business savings. Really these are rather astonishing figures when we consider them in connection with the proposals of our Minister of Finance. There was a total increase in gross business savings of rather more than $400 million between the years 1961 and 1962. This was made up of an increase of $200 million in undistributed corporation profits and a similar amount, multiplied by ten, with regard to depreciation allowances, which rose from $4,539 million in 1961 to $4,755 million in 1962.
I suggest, sir, that in the face of these figures the government and the Minister of Finance could have done much more toward dealing with the other problems that he has been presenting to us. In the main the two problems'-and his attempts to grapple with them, I may say, have my heartiest sympathy and support-are the question of foreign ownership and the question of reversing the rather disastrous centripetal force that has been dragging all our industry, all our production into only a few industrial centres. We face the problem of encouraging development in the designated areas and making some attempt to control the increasing foreign ownership of our resources and our industry.

As I say, Mr. Speaker, I have great sympathy, as I am sure practically every member of this house must have, with the minister when he tells us, quite rightly, that this is a very serious problem which may have results much more quickly than many of us understand and realize with regard to our political independence, as well as our economic independence. I think this is something that all Canadians should be recognizing today. We should be recognizing that we have actually only two courses to follow. We can attempt to do it along the lines that the minister has pointed out-and I am going to deal with the methods he has outlined, which I think are ineffective-or allow ourselves to be submerged in the economy and the political life of our great neighbour to the south. If we decide we are going to do the latter, the sensible thing for us to do would be to start negotiations to that end right now. If we are going to allow ourselves to be absorbed, let us take some positive action to be absorbed on our own terms. I think that idea is repugnant to most Canadians, but it is not sufficient merely to feel it is repugnant; you have to do something positive about it.
What the minister is suggesting in this bill is, I think, really a rather naively optimistic course of action. I refer to the suggestion that with great effort and, according to him this afternoon, the lapse, of considerable time, we might achieve a 25 per cent ownership in industries that are now foreign owned. As I say, I think it is naively optimistic in a day and age when it is notorious that even the majority stockholders in corporations have little or no say in their direction to imagine that a minority group of 25 per cent could have any really effective control over corporation policies. It is naive and optimistic in the extreme.
I would suggest that this suggestion has come about because of the government's preoccupation with some of the disappearing myths of economics from which we are still suffering; the idea that we must rely on private enterprise for all these changes which we wish to make. This not only produces an ineffective solution, but one that even if we achieve it today, tomorrow we might lose it; because if we are going to replace private American ownership-we might as well place the name right now on the record, because we all know to whom we are referring when we speak of foreign ownership-with private Canadian ownership, what guarantee have we that next week or next month or six months from now our Canadian 25 per cent ownership is not going to succumb to an attractive offer from the corporation directors of the company in which they hold their shares.

Income Tax Act
I would suggest that rather than do that, the minister would be better advised to lay plans for making a modest public investment, possibly even less than 25 per cent, in these industries in which it becomes possible to do so. He should take a leaf out of the book of the French planners, who have planned in a rather careful and rather conservative manner but who nevertheless have adopted a policy by legislation of ensuring that a designated director assumes his seat on the board of directors of every corporation in which the public authority invests funds in France. The steel industry in France, for instance, has about 30 per cent of its stock held by the public authority.
In addition to that, the public authority designates a director to take part in the deliberations of the board of directors of that Corporation. If you wish to make a minority stockholding effective on the board of directors you have to ensure, in the first place, that it is going to be permanently there, and in the second place that it will have a powerful voice on the board of directors.
I suggest that the director designated by the government of Canada would have a very important voice in any company decision. I also submit that the same argument must also be used with regard to this vexed question of encouraging development in the designated areas. In the first place, I think that some of the provisions are open to very severe criticism in that they appear to leave the door open for very substantial raids on the public treasury, by means of this tax exemption, by corporations-and I see nothing in the act which seems to prohibit this- which are well established in other parts of the country setting up a wholly-owned Subsidiary corporation, moving into one of these designated areas and taking advantage of these tax exemption provisions. It may be I am wrong and that I have read the bill wrongly, but I have not seen any provision there which would prevent that sort of operation. When we consider that the vast bulk of productive enterprise in Canada today is carried on by very large, powerful and wealthy corporations, I think this is a very real danger which faces the minister's attempts to encourage development in these designated areas.
These are the main criticisms I make of the minister's bill; but in addition I feel that the whole tax structure should really be reorganized and that it should be reorganized from an entirely different point of view from that which seems to be held by the government and by the minister. It should be considered part of the duty of a modern government and a modern minister of finance to use the budget and taxation, the fiscal structure

of the country, in a redistribution of income throughout the community. After all, that is the modern trend in society all over the world. It has been the means by which we have progressed. It has only been the rapid and quite drastic redistribution of income in North America which has enabled the North American economies to develop as they have. One of the pioneers, of course, in that field was a gentleman who would have repelled most vigorously any idea that that really had been his purpose, the late Henry Ford, who staggered and dismayed his fellow industrialists by suggesting that it was possible to pay $5 a day for industrial workers. When he did so he laid the groundwork for this redistribution of income upon which modern industry is now based; and I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the minister is missing an opportunity when he persists in increasing the benefits to be derived by wealthy corporations from our fiscal structure, and does nothing, or practically nothing, to advance this process of income redistribution upon which economic prosperity so largely depends.
Somebody mentioned this afternoon that the minister's attempt to deal with foreign ownership by means of his 30 per cent takeover tax had had to be abandoned, and then the Americans had moved into that field. I am sure the minister does not have that rather naive interpretation of the events which happened. I should like to speak for a moment on this, because it is one of the great problems facing us today.
The minister has pointed out that, due to the present position of the interest equalization tax, the legislation governing which is still undecided before the U.S. congress, there has been a virtual drying up of all investment coming into Canada, or at least a very severe diminution of it. The anxiety at the time the tax was announced to get special concessions from the United States indicated the minister's realization of the very precarious position in which the Canadian economy finds itself today. It is a precarious state of affairs because we have allowed ourselves to get into the position of depending upon a continual inflow of capital to balance our payments problem. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that there is something much more important which will have to be done than merely trying to keep United States investment out, or to diminish it, and to keep United States imports out if we are to tackle this whole problem which was indicated to us when President Kennedy announced the tax. It was in fact nothing less than an indication from the United States authorities that they are no longer able to do what they have been doing since 1945, and that is in large measure to finance the exchange transactions

of the world. It has been accomplished at the cost of enormous and growing deficits in the United States, which in turn have caused a weakening of the dollar, which again in turn has caused the run on gold which so alarmed the United States authorities.
My great fear is that Canada-although I must say I have seen no indication that the minister is moving in this direction-and other countries in the world may be tempted to seek a solution to this problem by unilateral action in order to preserve their own currency, and solve their own balance of payments problem unilaterally by a belttightening process. Unfortunately there are some very powerful and influential voices in Canada at the present time urging our Minister of Finance to pursue that policy. I hope he is going to turn a very deaf ear to those voices and is not going to put Canada in the position of taking part in what could only be a chain reaction of depression, such as took place some 30 years ago with the collapse of the pound sterling, when the world faced the same situation, and was under the same pressures and difficulties as are faced by the U.S. dollar today. Not that I am suggesting that the United States dollar is in any danger whatever of collapsing in the way the pound sterling did because, of course, the United States economy is still the wealthiest and most productive in the world. But the United States has given us and the other 21 nations in the world to whom the proposed legislation will apply notice that they can no longer shoulder this burden, and I hope the Canadian government will at least encourage, and perhaps take the lead in pressing for an international solution to this problem, an international solution which is required not merely to prevent the developed countries from plunging into a wave of depression, but also to make effective any development of the undeveloped areas of the world, or to provide any effective means of closing the gap which now is widening between the "have not" nations and "have" nations.
I think that these are the problems facing one minister. I hope he is going to resist the pressures which will be brought to bear on him to balance our budget, to tighten our belts to protect the Canadian dollar by the time-honoured method of balancing the budget and that he realizes that the world has now reached the stage where we have to cooperate with an international field and develop international mechanisms to deal with the economic problems of each of our national economies.
I feel that this bill before us this evening takes very little cognizance of the difficulties
Income Tax Act
which lie before us. I do not think we are going to be able to solve the problem of foreign ownership by the type of proposal brought forward by the minister. I think it is a much more far reaching problem which is going to require much more fundamental reorganization of our own economy. I would plead with the Minister of Finance and his colleagues that they do not fall into the stance adopted last night by one of our Conservative colleagues in the house, who launched such doughty blows for free enterprise that he wanted us to hand over Northern Transportation to private enterprise. I hope they will realize that so far from that being a sensible or rational procedure, the very reverse is required today-a great stepping up of public investment both independently and in conjunction with private investment. If we are to solve these problems of foreign ownership and the necessity of developing the designated areas, I trust the minister and his colleagues will bear that in mind and will not cast too many sidelong glances toward the gods of free enterprise, which are disappearing in the mists today, but leave their sacrifices before the new gods of collectivism which are beginning to emerge in the minds of intelligent and able people. -that the minister himself, as the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) just said, does not understand too well, although in private life he is an accountant and one of the best in Canada.
