Mr. Speaker, I submit that the minister-I recall talking about it here before, when the minister agreed to our request-should make an effort and try to trim down this whole tax legislation in order to make it more understandable for all Canadians, not only the ordinary taxpayers, but also those who pay large amounts in taxes, such as the companies, big or small, because it is legislation which is expensive to carry out since it requires too many people to fill out the tax returns.
If you try to read this legislation, you find it so difficult sometimes that some businessmen get discouraged, which I can understand, in preparing their annual returns.
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would urge the minister to simplify the act in order to make its contents clear to taxpayers, so that the businessman will not always be the victim of the official who, in most cases, is stone-hearted. Equipped with all the powers and privileges, he breaks into the businessman's office, carrying away all the papers with him. I see that the Minister of Finance is nodding. In fact, these officials may even arrive with trucks, empty safes and desks, and carry

everything with them. If the person objects, the Royal Mounted Police come 12 hours later with a warrant and take everything.
But if the act was simplified, if taxpayers were allowed to understand it better, if it was applied with more sense and heart, then Canadian citizens would be in a better situation. Today they not only pay but they have to put up with a lot of trouble.
By trying over and over again to make out what this is all about, Mr. Speaker, I finally succeeded in understanding certain points.
There is one in particular which I was able to make out. Indeed, the minister, at one point, quoted section 28 amending section 139 to make it section 139a (1):
For the purpose of this act, a corporation has a degree of Canadian ownership and control in a taxation year if throughout the 60 day period immediately preceding that year (or if the corporation did not have a preceding taxation year, throughout the 60 day period commencing on the first day of the year).
And it continues:
(a) the corporation complied with the following conditions:
(i)	the corporation was resident in Canada,
(ii)	either
(A) not less than 25 per cent of the issued shares of the corporation having full voting rights were owned by one or more individuals resident in Canada-
Then, the minister stated that, more or less, he was satisfied that a corporation is controlled and owned by Canadians if 25 per cent of the issued shares are owned by Canadians. It does not take much to satisfy him, because 25 per cent of the shares are owned by Canadians while 75 per cent are owned by non-residents. And the minister claims that those corporations would be controlled by Canadians.
If we keep on accepting that corporations can get special privileges while 75 per cent of their shares are owned by foreigners, or foreign corporations, we should not be surprised to see foreigners monopolizing 75 per cent of the shares of Canadian corporations in order to enjoy special privileges.
I submit that if we want to grant some rights or privileges to those corporations, it must be to corporations in which at least 51 per cent of the shares, not 25 per cent, are owned by Canadian interests, so that the policies may be decided on here, in Canada.
This is what I read in a newspaper today:
Washington proposes to Ottawa the establishment of a vast natural resources pool.
Canada has natural resources such as iron, oil, etc. It would seem that the Americans would like to set up a pool of our natural resources to get as much as they can from our own resources. Who would thereby benefit?

If this bill is adopted and if we stipulate that only 25 per cent of the shares of Canadian companies are to be held by our nationals, who would benefit from such a pool of our natural resources?
Mr. Speaker, I say that it is the United States or American financiers who would again profit from such a scheme.
In the financial columns of the same newspaper, the Quebec premier is reported as saying:
Canadian capital is not sufficient, said Mr. Le-sage, if we are to fulfil our dreams. Foreign capital will be required to carry out the projects which Quebec's future justifies.
There would seem to be some contradiction between the statement of the Quebec premier and the proposal made by the federal Minister of Finance who is trying to repatriate our industries. One of them says: "Let us regain control of our economy" while the other states that we must attract foreign capital. There does not seem to be any common ground for agreement between them, since the Minister of Finance would like to see Canadians take over the control of their industry, even if the proportion is to be only 25 per cent, while the Quebec premier claims that our dreams cannot be fulfilled nor our projects carried out if we do not get financial assistance from outside, because there is not enough capital here to develop our country.
We must welcome foreign capital in order to achieve our goals. Investments are needed.
If, instead of exerting so much effort to find foreign capital, the Minister of Finance would try to create capital in Canada, which is something we are in a position to do, then Canadians could develop themselves, for the benefit of Canadians, the natural resources available in our own country.
We have all the resources, the manpower and the skills required. Yesterday, the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) told us to find some competent people. We claim that such people exist; we know that there are competent people able to develop our natural resources. But what do we need then? Only the financial means to develop our natural resources.
I fail to understand why a supposedly intelligent group, such as the present cabinet with so many economists, is unable to find a solution where mere figures or scraps of paper will no longer impede the development of our Canadian resources.
I wonder why the Minister of Finance, who is a good accountant, has not yet realized that, by means of a monetary and financial system, it is possible to develop the natural resources of our country without always having to beg from foreigners a few scraps of
Income Tax Act
paper that are needed to put people to work in our country for the development of our resources.
This is completely incomprehensible. How is it that the required capital is not available in our country?
Here is what Malraux says:
Andre Malraux makes a summary of his mission.
My predominating impression about Quebec? Hope.
What struck me about your achievements? Their intentions.
Hope for the future. Intentions.
Intentions are good. There is hope of seeing them come true. But why is it not done? Why are our intentions not brought into being? Precisely because, in Canada, we are somewhat limited in our plans for lack of funds. When we need money, we are forced to go and beg abroad, outside of our own borders.
That problem has been raised several times in the house already. We have tried to explain our ideas understood in various ways. To us the matter appears simple. The Minister of Finance listens to us but, so far, he has not done a thing.
We find it strange that, whenever the government tries to do something, for instance to increase old age pensions, it always has the same idea in mind, that is to increase taxes. That is a step it promises to avoid prior to the election but, once the election is over, it does the opposite.
And now I shall deal quickly with another point. Reference has been made to receipts for charitable donations. I agree with what was said a while ago, to the effect that an abnormal situation is developing in this field. I get letters from my electors and other people who say: "We have sent receipts duly signed by the parish priest and, without telling us why, an income tax inspector has taken it upon himself to reduce the amount of money coming to us."
If only the inspector would go and see the taxpayer and explain to him the reason for this reduction; but no, the amount of the refund is reduced without consultation with anyone.
The small taxpayer has two alternatives: either accept the situation-and he is squashed once more-or start procedures to get his due, which will entail expenses.
When the Department of National Revenue cuts down the charitable donation receipts, the taxpayer should not have to pay the costs of the proceedings.
The department acts in a dictatorial way when it cuts down the refund and makes the taxpayer bear the costs of the proof. It is

Income Tax Act
contrary to the law, in Canada. The Minister of National Revenue acts in a way which is contrary to the provisions of the Civil Code of the province of Quebec, and contrary to the law in Canada. While our law is based on the principle that the onus of proof lies with the prosecutor, it lies upon the taxpayer in the case of income tax, and this contrary to the provisions of Canadian law.
The result of this is that the small taxpayer is satisfied with staying home and grumbling against the Department of National Revenue and the government.
Why not change the procedure. When the department receives an income tax return, why not accept it as it is? It is true that some taxpayers try to cheat, but then the onus of proving the cheating or error should lie with the Department of National Revenue. The department should not make an arbitrary decision by itself, saying to the small taxpayer: "If you are not satisfied, take proceedings, even if this is costly."
The Department of National Revenue forces too many Canadians to suffer injustice and keep quiet, because they do not have the means to defend themselves. As far as charity receipts are concerned, I am of the opinion that the stand of the department is unfair. I suggest the inspectors of the federal government have really been trained to act as dictators and give as much trouble as possible to our Canadian citizens. That situation should change, and we take advantage of this opportunity to request an amendment to the Income Tax Act.
I should like to speak again of a certain argument which is very important to us and which we mentioned often. I will deal quickly with it because there is not much time left; it is the ultimatum of the premier of Quebec. That ultimatum was delivered April 5 last, that is six months ago. There are only six months left until April 5, 1964.
The Quebec premier has delivered an ultimatum to the federal government, whatever may be the party in power after the general election of April 8, demanding that the federal government give back to the province of Quebec, as a first step and before April 5, 1964, 25 per cent of personal income taxes, 25 per cent of corporation taxes and 100 per cent of succession duties. On coming back here after the election, we asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chevrier) if they were aware of the ultimatum.
What was their reaction? We were told: "No, we never heard about it". And a few days later, after having received some newspaper clippings with the following headlines:
[Mr. Gregoire.l
The ultimatum of the province of Quebec-
They admitted that there was an ultimatum. Today, the government knows there is an ultimatum and it is aware that this ultimatum ends on April 5 next.
There is a lot of talk about saving confederation. If we wish to save it, let us begin by abiding by it, by respecting the two great races forming Canada and at the same time by respecting one another.
I read in the same newspaper:
Lamontagne is confident that Canada will survive its centennial.
This is the President of the Privy Council, the member for Outremont-St. Jean (Mr. Lamontagne), talking.
If we wish to ensure the survival of confederation, we must begin by respecting it, which implies the enforcement of the British North America Act which gives direct taxes such as corporation taxes and succession duties to the provinces.
Those fields of taxation belong to the provinces, and the federal government has now but six months to satisfy the terms and conditions given in this ultimatum which has our support, as a first step, for our struggle will come to an end only if and when we get back 100 per cent of our revenue sources.
Should this government be unwilling to face the present situation, to have regard for the spirit as well as for the letter of confederation, then, we shall have the right to say-and I will be the first one to do so, I say it once more-we shall have the right to say that our confederation will suffer a break and will perhaps be unable to celebrate its centennial. I, for one, will not hesitate to say so.
If the intention is to give back to the provinces what belongs to them in the first place, that is the sources of revenues to which they are entitled, I, for one, will have increased confidence in confederation. But if the situation does not change shortly, then, I will say that confederation is a situation where the central government tries to deprive the provincial governments in an attempt to appropriate all fields such as education, health, hospitalization plans, etc.
If the intention is not to carry out the undertakings given in the British North America Act, I will not hesitate in stating that. I shall say that confederation did not attain its goal and that it is a colossal failure.
However, we hope that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) will assume his responsibilities and will revamp his system so as to restitute to the provinces the income tax, the corporations profits tax and the succession duties.

Mr. Malraux is right when he says:
What strikes me most in the province of Quebec is their intentions.
We have intentions in the province of Quebec, we have faith in French Canadian people, we intend to develop our province, our ethnic group. We are confident because we know that we are able to do it; we have faith in our own people, and we are able to help develop the country as a whole.
But if they start by not abiding by the commitments of the past, those resulting from the confederation, if they start by taking away from us the means to develop ourselves, how can we carry out those intentions?
What prevails at this time in the province of Quebec is a feeling of hope. We hope to find our own way towards development, within the frame of our own culture, to which we are deeply attached, and without betrayal of our French Canadian personality. We intend to develop our province, our ethnical group. If we are deprived of the necessary means towards that end, we shall have to take whatever measures are available.
I have perhaps deviated somewhat from the subject of the Income Tax Act, but not too much, really, because what we want is that the power of taxation be given back to the province of Quebec, as well as to all the other provinces.
Mr. Speaker, those are the few remarks I wanted to make to clarify all those complicated things, like our monetary system, which nobody understands in Canada, and also, in order to simplify the Income Tax Act, so that the minister might, by resorting to efficient means and not to 25 per cent measures, succeed in Canadianizing our industries, our manufactures and our natural resources, by taking the necessary steps to give a positive answer to the ultimatum delivered not by a political party, but by the whole people of Quebec, and which will expire on April 8 next.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (Minister of Industry):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Hales) made some observations in relation to designated areas. In particular, he suggested that the scheme which had been introduced for designating areas was discriminatory. In the dictionary sense of the word, this is quite true. The scheme and the criteria are designed to be discriminatory, to pick out the less fortunate, the more unfavoured areas, and to provide measures of assistance for them over and above what the Canadian economy provides for Canada as a whole. In this sense, it is discriminatory and it is deliberately discriminatory.
28902-5-233
Income Tax Act
An endeavour has been made through the criteria to select those areas which have been the least favoured in terms of a chronic high level of unemployment and stagnation, in terms of economic growth, and to provide advantages to those areas which will enable them, to some extent, to offset the disadvantages and to share to a greater degree in our national growth, in our national prosperity, than has been the case in the past. The hon. member mentioned that Brantford, particularly the N.E.S. area, should not be allowed to continue to be designated and draw these advantages. He suggested that the people of Brantford did not like their area being described as a designated area. I can assure him that I have heard from the mayor of Brantford. Although he is unable to speak for the whole of the N.E.S. area, the mayor of Brantford is highly appreciative of the fact that Brantford is in the national employment service designated area.
Perhaps some citizens of more fortunate communities would prefer not to see these advantages go to the more unfortunate sister communities, and I suppose this is understandable. I do not suggest this is a reason for the federal government giving way and yielding to those who suggest that we should not exercise our responsibility by providing what measures of assistance we can to relieve the chronic high level of unemployment and assist in accelerating the economic growth of less favoured areas.
I should like, Mr. Speaker, to provide a few figures in respect of this particular question. I may say that of the 35 areas designated in respect of high level unemployment in the summer months, not one has registered anything except satisfaction at the plan. The community of Guelph and its contiguous areas are the only ones from whom representations have been received protesting the plan. As Minister of Industry, I have received a vast number of representations urging that additional communities should be included, and in particular the communities represented by the speaker. However, they do accept the fact it is necessary to qualify under the criteria and consequently they do not press.
The criteria which have been criticized provide as follows: That an N.E.S. area will qualify for designation, and consequently assistance which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) has outlined, if it has suffered from a high level of chronic unemployment and a lack of economic growth. This, in concrete terms, means that during the six summer months from May to October an area must have been in the labour surplus category for over 50 per cent of those months during the past eight years. Further, that over the past

Income Tax Act
eight years it must have recorded a rate of growth less than half the national average.
I will compare two cities, Brantford and Guelph, during this eight year period. During the 48 summer months in the past eight years, 1955-62, Brantford was in a labour surplus condition for 87 per cent of those months. During the same period of 48 months Guelph was in a labour surplus condition for only 21 per cent of those months.
During the same eight years the rate of employment growth in Brantford was 2 per cent; that is, 2 per cent over the whole eight years. During the same period Guelph experienced a growth in employment of 19.7 per cent, almost ten times as great.
A second criterion is related to communities which, while they may have been relatively well off over the long haul, have experienced a sudden decrease in industrial activity. In this case a criterion has been established for looking at only a three year period, and in order to qualify under the three year period a N.E.S. area must have been for 18 summer months of that period in a surplus labour condition for 50 per cent of those months.
In the last three years, 1959-62, Brantford was in a labour surplus condition in 89 per cent of the summer months, and Guelph was in a labour surplus condition in only 39 per cent of those same 18 months. In the same three years the growth of employment in Brantford, on a minus or negative growth basis, showed minus 7.4 per cent, while in the same three years the growth of employment in Guelph was plus 2.4 per cent.
Taking it year by year in those three years, employment changes in Brantford in 1959-60 compared with the previous year were minus 7 per cent; 1960-61, minus 6.1 per cent, and in 1961-62 a plus of 1.2 per cent. I say this to indicate that in the last year there was some slight improvement in the Brantford employment picture. However in the same period in Guelph the growth of employment was 4.7 per cent, about four times as great.

May I ask the minister a question. He is talking about Brantford being a depressed area, but why should it be, when recently two firms had advertisements in the Kitchener-Waterloo Record asking for labour help?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would draw the attention of the house to the fact that the use of the term "depressed area" was not employed by me. Brantford is not a depressed area.
Well, distressed.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
Nor is it distressed. There is a rate of high unemployment and slow economic

growth, and I suggest the reason employers in Brantford have been advertising outside of Brantford for help probably lies in the fact that the shortage of skilled artisans throughout Canada is well known and recognized. If we have high unemployment it is unemployment of those who are unskilled.
In many categories of industrial employment there is a labour shortage in Canada today, and part of the problem we face as a country is to convert those who are unskilled into those possessed of skills. While in Brantford today there is a great surplus of manpower unemployment there is no surplus- indeed I suspect there is a shortage-in certain skilled categories.

May I ask the minister a question. Is he not aware that in the city of Brantford there are rather peculiar or exceptional circumstances which have created this statistical unemployment picture during the last two years, and when I say statistical I mean in comparison to its neighbouring communities? I refer of course to the relocation of the Massey-Ferguson Company and the Cockshutt Company. It is perhaps worthy to note that Brantford over the years has been largely dependant on the farm machinery business, and because of the relocation and rebuilding of these big plants this has probably created a very decided aberration in these unemployment figures.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: I do not accept the suggestion that because there have been plants closed in Brantford as a consequence of relocation of industry, and as a consequence of this a lot of people were unemployed, that this created an aberration in the unemployment figures.
They are building a $15 million plant in Brantford now. That is the reason.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: I might point out to the hon. member that during the current summer, while this multimillion dollar plant was being built, there were probably more people employed in the construction force than would be employed when the plant comes into operation. The figures I have given to the house related to the current summer months while this high level, or allegedly high level of construction activity has been going on in Brantford. When these buildings are completed those in the construction trades engaged in building the plants will be laid off. They will be replaced by the people operating these plants, but there will still be the same number displaced in the unemployment roles as those now engaged in the construction industry and who will be laid off when building is completed.
May I suggest to the minister that these construction people are not from Brantford but from other cities.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock?
I suggest to hon. members that in view of the letter we have received from the other place we should stay for a few minutes more. I have been informed that the messenger is on his way.

May I ask the minister another question. If you have Brantford as a distressed area instead of a depressed area, do you not feel all the cities in that community are going to suffer in regard to new industries?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: I did not quite get the question. Do I feel that because Brantford has been designated, then other sections of that community will suffer-is that the question?
Yes, the other cities in the community, Kitchener, Waterloo, Preston and Guelph. I am sure they will suffer by not being able to secure more industries.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
There is no question that Brantford is going to have a temporary advantage. After all, one of the purposes of the legislation is to confer an advantage on an area which for some reason or another has suffered over past years. The intention is to provide additional assistance to relieve high level chronic unemployment. It will have an advantage, but I do not feel for a second, nor do I think the hon. member does, that this advantage is going to be such that all industry coming to Canada is going to locate in Brant-
Business of the House
ford and, as a consequence, all other cities in Canada might as well shut up shop.
I do not expect that at all.
